LOCKDOWN Grapes of Wrath

By: Liz Fish | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Wine exports represent R9 billion in foreign earnings and stopping wine exports has cost South Africa R3 billion

Unique Selling Point:
The wine industry in the Western Cape exports 50% of their wines and so when lockdown was announced, and all their domestic income cut off, they had a lifeline. They could export to the overseas markets which were booming and had taken years to establish. Lockdown came at the end of a bumper harvest where both volumes and quality were excellent and they manged to bring in the crop. Then suddenly 9 days later, Minister Dhlamini Zuma and Minister of Transport Fikile Mbalula shut it all down. Bottle stores were looted and a container hijacked and that was the end of the lifeline. It’s made no sense and as wine farms have pointed out that it takes 3 people to export and none of them have to have any contact with each other. The wine industry has even offered to escort their goods to the harbour under heavy security.

Summary:
They are losing R200 million weekly and 70 to 80 of the smaller wineries are in danger of collapsing. 98% of wine is produced in the Cape and they employ nearly 300 000 people, and that does not include all the other industries they support like tourism and the restaurant trade. Not only have they lost income in March and April but they are likely not to get much income for the next 4 or 5 months as wine sales take 60 to 90 days to pay. The impcats will be felt for years to come as they have already lost valuable listing in Europe. SA is the only wine producing country in the world not allowed to export wine, and wine sales are booming under lockdown in America and Europe. It will take decades to win back those listings as they can’t even send them tastings for this year. Normally at this time of the year they are travelling the European and American markets marketing their wines in the European summer. The wine industry is extremely competitive and their hard-earned market share is disappearing by the day while Chile and Argentina fill the gap.






Further information:
Last year after the drought SA exported 320 million liters but in a good year 420 million liters. Even if they can export on the 1st May they won’t see any income for another couple of months as the payment cycle is 60 days. Locally the restaurants returned their wines and got their cash back when they saw what was coming. It’s possible that there will be no income in the next 6 months if local wine sales don’t open up.

Most wine farms have guest houses and restaurants and all that income has collapsed. Wine tours form a major part of the local tourism industry. They also play a pivotal role in the rural economy supporting local schools and feeding schemes. Many farms can keep paying workers till the end of May and then they face massive retrenchments as they have had no income for the last 3 months.

Consol glass has been heavily hit not being able to supply bottles to the beer or wine industry and there is concern that they may only be able to supply bottles for export orders which means wine makers could well be left half used vats of wine which will go to waste. Local label printers and not able to print alcohol labels so even if bottling is allowed they cannot complete the process.

The devil is in the detail with the disaster regulations. Alcohol may not be transported so even if exports are allowed can they transport the wine? Wine farms are supporting the feeding schemes but hot food cannot be transported- so despite 40 local chefs cooking for the feeding schemes they have to let the food get cold and then distribute cold meals.



Extra Budget Items:
The wine farms are out of town the one day will cover 160km Wellington, Paarl, Stellenbosch. Day two Stellenbosch Constantia, Bellville is 110 km

Press Release:


Lockdown in the Winelands
With around 600 wineries affected by lockdown, the iconic Cape winelands that earn R49 billion for the country annually are bleeding revenue, jobs and prospects. COVID-19 lockdown regulations saw alcohol sales and exports shut down. It came after the harvest was in – it had been a good year with increased volumes and quality. This was supposed to be the time to recover heavy capital investments early in the season and reverse the difficult years of drought. Carte Blanche examines what it will take to recover hope in the industry.
Producer: Liz Fish | Presenter: Claire Mawisa


Script:


LINK Because of the local ban on alcohol, by now it’s quite possible you have run out of wine and craving a glass. But in the rest of the world, drinkers are taking the edge off lockdown anxiety by drinking and online wine sales are booming! But local wine producers are desperate, and if something doesn’t shift soon many will go under
Script: Denise Stubbs returned to a small wine farm in Wellington for the 1st time since lockdown to talk to us
Denise I think this morning when I walked into this gate, it was very emotional for me to see the quietness of this farm
Script: Denise is the child of farm labourers and grew up with the dop system, today she is the MD of Thokozani wines, a small development winery based on Diemersfontein wine farm where the 75workers are shareholders
Denise The impact of COVID 19 on this farm is horrific.. We've gone through so with the recession, with the drought, and suddenly we've got this disease and the uncertainty of not knowing where we're going. And I think all the regulations and restrictions with government is putting us in almost a horror movie if I can say that
Script: They’ve worked hard to establish their name for fine wine, and to be recognized as far more than an empowerment project. This year’s harvest was good, and now was the time to recoup their costs.
Denise And suddenly we stuck, we can't bottle, we can't label, we can't sell, so the impact is severe. And we as Tokozani have an exclusivity with Woolworths being 85 percent of our income. And suddenly, my goodness, there's nothing. I actually get goosebumps saying this, nothing in the sense of nothing.
Script: No restaurant, accommodation, or wine sales. And she is not alone, 80% of the 600 wineries in the Western Cape are small SME enterprises. Half of them have restaurants and accommodation, so they have lost all their income streams. Lars Maack of Buitenvervating in Constantia, says it’s the uncertainty that’s giving him sleepless nights.
Lars “I fully understand why Ramaphosa is doing it and ……...for most of the restrictions we believe they are right. But you can't do this for indefinite. So we have responsibilities to our staff, and we need to have a kind of a roadmap, to plan our business forward, otherwise you've got to ask yourself is there still a business.
Script:The iconic Cape winelands earns R49 billion for the country annually, and is the 2nd largest employer in the Western Cape, with just under 300 000 people
Link: Half of South African wines are exported and so when alcohol sales were banned under lockdown locally wine producers still had a life line, but it was a short lived, suddenly after frantically getting wine to ports exports were stopped overnight leaving the wine industry high and dry
Lars: we are a white wine producer and Northern hemisphere is going now into white wine season and 40 percent of our sales are export, but it is quite distorted because that 40 percent would be all happening now, that's hurting us really badly. Plus you also have it's not only that you that you lose those sales now but you're also losing shelf space. And in some instances you have only that one week or two week period where like a mail order company they would want a big story on us …..and you have no wine to deliver you lose that gap completely
Script: And the frustration is, this could have been avoided, if Government had just allowed wines to be transported to the ports, which had minimal impact on people’s health, explains Rico Basson MD of Vinpro, which represents two and half thousand wine growers and wineries
Rico The reasons were it's due to high levels of criminality. …. you would think that if that is the case in a consultative process, such as let's look at ways to safeguard these containers going to harbor. Let's look at ways to truck them in a convoy.
Link: It’s taken over 30 years to build the South Africa wine industry internationally and we were the only wine producing country in the world that stopped exports due to our lockdown regulations. Sales in America and Europe however are booming, especially online. With exports banned they watched hard fought for shelf space slip away, contracts lost, and orders not filled
Siobhan The problem is if you don't have a bottle on shelf to sell so that space is going to be taken up by a competitor and it's going to be very difficult to get that back.
Script: Siobhan Thompson of Wines of South Africa, the industry body whose task it is to promote wines internationally, says R 2billion in sales was lost in April, and the full cost will take time to calculate
Siobhan: We've also got summer promotions in markets in the European markets and the North American markets and they running their consumer promotions in stores and we're not going to necessarily have the wine to compete with the other countries at this critical time.
LINK Lifting the ban on exports was widely celebrated with the move to level 4, but the backlog at the harbour will take weeks to clear, with only two of the 4 loading berths operating, and months before it gets to the market and producers get real money in their pockets.
Script: And right now, it looks like 13% of the wine producers could go under, that’s 14000 jobs lost immediately. 80 smaller wineries are at risk, because not all producers export, some are almost exclusively dependent on the local market like Thokozani wines
Denise [19:40:54] For the past two years, we've been really focused on exports and we were ready this year. 2020 was our year that we want to fly. And we really were ready. But now how can I say 5 percent maybe of the A ninety five percent versus local sales. But there's nothing at the moment and that 5 percent is not gonna survive Tokozani
Script: And Thokozani Wines are dependent on wine entrepreneurs like Clive Hlabathi, but many have already gone under. Clive’s passion it is to educate people about those smaller unknown wines
Upsound Clive “Over here we have got one of the few black wine makers……he follows a more natural wine making regiment which means no added sulphites, no synthetic yeast used
Claire”I like that only grapes went into this wine”
Clive That’s it
Claire: Are you thinking about how you are going to do business differently?
Clive: 16 25 Wine tasting will have to take on a more of a technological or virtual format. Where wines will now get delivered to you.. and we will all log into Zoom and we will crack open a bottle of wine and somebody will conduct a tasting, we are going to have to be more rigorous of taking wine to the people
Script: But when is the question they're all asking? The current Government position is that it’s keeping trauma wards free of accident victims from alcohol abuse, and drinking leads to unsociable behaviour.
Rico [21:26:26] I think that's almost a frustration that we do think there are common ground, even on local sales. Where with a low risk fazingin approach certain things like E-Trade. Like home delivery with food. Even in licensed grocers, we can limit the volumes..
Script: Even Distell, one of the biggest local players is taking strain. They buy 35% of the grapes grown in this country, and 50% of the apple concentrate, as well as Maroela fruit from the small communities in Phalaborwa. CEO Richard Rushton says exports are only 27% of their income
Richard we currently have about R442 billion rands with a business on backorder waiting to supply so it's a substantial revenue generator both for the fiscus and the government. We'd be faced with a difficult balance of having to pay excise to government on the one hand yet also pay our employees and suppliers on the other. And trying to find that balancing act has being almost impossible
Script: And Rico is working hard to secure loans from commercial banks, to mitigate the crisis
Rico [21:22:27] The UIF benefit is there for the taking and I think a lot of the companies are using that. But beyond the that there is not a lot of schemes and assistance. We did ask for excise dispensation to extend that for 90 days. It was given it., it largely assisted some of the spirits company, not so much the wine companies.
Link: One of the unintended consequences of the ongoing ban of alcohol is the spike in the illicit trade, before lockdown one in four bottles was lost to the black market now during lockdown its spiralling out of control
Script: Johan Van Loggerenberg, former Group Executive for SARS Enforcement, points out that before lockdown we were losing 6.4 billion rand to illegal trade in cigarettes and alcohol, and those syndicates have just ramped up
Johan 00.21 37 But the worrying factor is that it's not just the money lost to the country it's about feeding into existing crime groupings and making them richer, pushing them more underground making them more powerful. Those older established networks are not going to go away,.and the new entrants who have seen South Africa as a massive market to introduce their product into will also not go away and so there will be a lot more crime dynamics at play
Script: We put these question to the DTI and requested an interview, but have not had a response.
Link: There is growing anger and frustration and as the alcohol ban stretches into the unforeseeable future, first it was just for 3 weeks but it's been 7 weeks and it’s still unclear when people can buy alcohol again
Script: Tholine Samuels, supervisor of Thokozani’s vineyard, sees the illegal wine trade everyday in her community. She's supporting 7 people, and struggling to do so on only 70% of her salary, she fears for Thokazani Wines future, and her hard earned dividends slipping away.
Tholine 20 34 43 02 If this wine can be sold and our wines can’t be sold what’s going to happen to us what’s going to happen to children's future. People out there don’ think its wrong and those people are getting rich and what about us
Denise Millions of people are already without jobs. We've got a high percentage of unemployment. I cannot afford our agriculture staff that's got the heart and soul and soil of this industry to suffer more

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Wine exports represent R9 billion in foreign earnings and stopping wine exports has cost South Africa R3 billion
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The wine industry in the Western Cape exports 50% of their wines and so when lockdown was announced, and all their domestic income cut off, they had a lifeline. They could export to the overseas markets which were booming and had taken years to establish. Lockdown came at the end of a bumper harvest where both volumes and quality were excellent and they manged to bring in the crop. Then suddenly 9 days later, Minister Dhlamini Zuma and Minister of Transport Fikile Mbalula shut it all down. Bottle stores were looted and a container hijacked and that was the end of the lifeline. It’s made no sense and as wine farms have pointed out that it takes 3 people to export and none of them have to have any contact with each other. The wine industry has even offered to escort their goods to the harbour under heavy security.
metadata.Summary: They are losing R200 million weekly and 70 to 80 of the smaller wineries are in danger of collapsing. 98% of wine is produced in the Cape and they employ nearly 300 000 people, and that does not include all the other industries they support like tourism and the restaurant trade. Not only have they lost income in March and April but they are likely not to get much income for the next 4 or 5 months as wine sales take 60 to 90 days to pay. The impcats will be felt for years to come as they have already lost valuable listing in Europe. SA is the only wine producing country in the world not allowed to export wine, and wine sales are booming under lockdown in America and Europe. It will take decades to win back those listings as they can’t even send them tastings for this year. Normally at this time of the year they are travelling the European and American markets marketing their wines in the European summer. The wine industry is extremely competitive and their hard-earned market share is disappearing by the day while Chile and Argentina fill the gap.
metadata.Further information: Last year after the drought SA exported 320 million liters but in a good year 420 million liters. Even if they can export on the 1st May they won’t see any income for another couple of months as the payment cycle is 60 days. Locally the restaurants returned their wines and got their cash back when they saw what was coming. It’s possible that there will be no income in the next 6 months if local wine sales don’t open up. Most wine farms have guest houses and restaurants and all that income has collapsed. Wine tours form a major part of the local tourism industry. They also play a pivotal role in the rural economy supporting local schools and feeding schemes. Many farms can keep paying workers till the end of May and then they face massive retrenchments as they have had no income for the last 3 months. Consol glass has been heavily hit not being able to supply bottles to the beer or wine industry and there is concern that they may only be able to supply bottles for export orders which means wine makers could well be left half used vats of wine which will go to waste. Local label printers and not able to print alcohol labels so even if bottling is allowed they cannot complete the process. The devil is in the detail with the disaster regulations. Alcohol may not be transported so even if exports are allowed can they transport the wine? Wine farms are supporting the feeding schemes but hot food cannot be transported- so despite 40 local chefs cooking for the feeding schemes they have to let the food get cold and then distribute cold meals.
